On July 16, 2026, the federal government announced it intends to introduce reforms to the Modern Slavery Act 2018 centered on a new criminal "failure to prevent" modern slavery offence for companies with over AUD 100 million revenue; this remains an announcement of intent only -- no bill has been tabled in Parliament -- and it would in any case be a corporate-liability offence, not an import prohibition. STALE-SOURCE GUARD (re-confirmed this run): search results periodically surface a headline that the Australian Senate "passed" a forced-labour import bill. That refers to Senator Rex Patrick's 2021/2022 private senator's bill, which lapsed before the 2022 election and never became law. It must not be treated as a current or enacted measure. Re-confirmed August 15, 2026 that the offence remains unlegislated and no bill has been tabled; the announcement is documented on the Attorney-General's own ministerial page. The July 16 'failure to prevent' offence remains at CONSULTATION stage, with the consultation now reported to close on SEPTEMBER 25, 2026 and no bill tabled -- so it stays No under the standing policy, which requires a measure to be tabled or published, not merely announced or consulted on. Source: USTR press release and White House presidential action, July 23, 2026.
Official Forced Labor Import Ban: No (Modern Slavery Act 2018 is a reporting regime, not an import prohibition; the announced "failure to prevent" offence is unlegislated and corporate-liability in nature, and the 2021 Senate private member's bill lapsed)

Summary and Source: STATUS CHANGE this run, No to Partial -- a policy-consistency correction, not a new event. Brazil has had a formally tabled forced-labour import-ban bill since 2015: PL 2.799/2015 (Dep. Davidson Magalhaes), which with PL 3717/2015 and PL 5072/2016 attached would prohibit importing and trading goods made with child, forced or compulsory labour, provide for seizure and forfeiture, and require the government to publish a six-monthly list of implicated companies drawing on ILO data and court decisions. Verified directly against the Chamber of Deputies' own tramitacao record (dadosabertos.camara.leg.br, 76 recorded events): the Labour Committee approved the rapporteur's substitutive on September 15, 2025 -- which expanded the original cocoa-only text to all products -- the Economic Development Committee (CDE) approved its parecer on June 10, 2026, and the bill was received by the Constitution, Justice and Citizenship Committee (CCJC) on June 12, 2026, where it is awaiting designation of a rapporteur. It is not enacted and still requires CCJC and Senate passage. Under the standing policy a formally tabled but unenacted import-ban bill is Partial, so the prior "No" was inconsistent with the classification rule rather than with the facts. Two dating corrections recorded: the CDE approval was June 10, 2026, not "the week of July 13" as this row previously stated, and the widely syndicated "committee approves" article is the Chamber's own September 15, 2025 story about the Labour Committee, not a 2026 item. Separately, Brazil's government (gov.br/Secom) called USTR's conclusion "regrettable," citing its ILO-recognised record; and a distinct, unrelated 25% Section 301 tariff (digital trade, ethanol, deforestation, IP) took effect July 22, 2026, on top of which the 12.5% forced-labour tariff was confirmed July 23, 2026. Source: Camara dos Deputados open-data tramitacao record and Camara news, September 15, 2025; gov.br/Secom; USTR press release, July 23, 2026.
Official Forced Labor Import Ban: Partial (PL 2.799/2015, with PL 3717/2015 and PL 5072/2016 attached, would prohibit importing and trading goods made with child/forced labour; substitutive approved by the Labour Committee September 15, 2025 and by the Economic Development Committee June 10, 2026, received by the Constitution and Justice Committee June 12, 2026 awaiting a rapporteur; not enacted, still requires CCJC and Senate passage)

Summary and Source: Canada has had a forced-labor import prohibition since July 1, 2020 (Customs Tariff item 9897.00.00) but USTR flagged weak enforcement (only 2 shipments ever actually prohibited). In response, Canada tabled Bill C-35 -- "An Act respecting the prohibition of the importation of goods produced by forced labour" -- on June 12, 2026, to strengthen the ban with a new supply-chain tracing framework. STAGE CLARIFIED this run against Parliament's own LegisInfo record, because it is easy to misread: the bill's status field reads "At second reading in the House of Commons," but its latest recorded event is still "Introduction and first reading" dated June 12, 2026, and its latest COMPLETED major stage is First reading. Under LegisInfo's convention the status names the stage a bill is awaiting, not one it has cleared -- so C-35 has NOT advanced, and no second-reading debate has occurred, with Parliament in summer recess. A future run should not read that status label as progress. The Global Affairs Canada/CBSA consultation on forced-labour import identification criteria and importer evidentiary requirements, and a parallel ESDC supply-chain due-diligence consultation, remain open and CLOSED ON AUGUST 21, 2026 -- THE CLOSING DATE FELL ON THIS RUN. Both consultations closed as scheduled with NO EXTENSION, corroborated across Baker McKenzie (August 19), Mondaq and Norton Rose Fulbright commentary and against Global Affairs Canada's own consultation page; no "what we heard" report, outcome statement or next-step announcement has been published as at the close. Re-checked on August 22, 23, 24 and 25: still no outcome report, summary of submissions or next-step announcement from Global Affairs Canada, CBSA or ESDC, and no major stakeholder submissions published. SEPARATE AND MUCH LARGER DEVELOPMENT, retrieved and read directly from the Prime Minister's own statement of August 21, 2026 (pm.gc.ca, Ottawa): Canada has SUSPENDED its trade negotiations with the United States. Carney states, "this evening, I have decided to suspend trade negotiations with the U.S. and have directed Canada's negotiators to return to Ottawa," citing "last-minute changes in the U.S. proposed terms" that "were unfair, uneconomic, and called into question the reliability of any deal," and adds that "At midnight tonight, the U.S. intends to impose a 50% tariff on roughly $28 billion of Canadian goods. Canada will match those tariffs dollar for dollar." TWO THINGS THIS DOES NOT MEAN, both worth stating because they are easy to conflate. First, this is a SEPARATE tariff track from the Section 301 forced-labour action this tracker follows: Canada's 10% forced-labour tier is unaffected by it. Second, because no agreement was concluded, no new US-Canada instrument exists and so nothing here creates an RTA forced-labour commitment -- the statement contains no reference to forced labour at all, which I confirmed against the full text. Canada's classification rests where it always has, on the enacted 2020 prohibition. The suspension does, however, remove for now any prospect of a negotiated instrument carrying a forced-labour clause, and it makes the pending consultation outcome the only live domestic thread in this row. SEQUENCE CLARIFIED AND EXTENDED as of August 26, still on that separate track: negotiators had actually reconvened in Washington on August 20 before talks failed again, Carney reconfirmed the suspension on August 22, and Canada then announced retaliatory tariffs on August 25 covering roughly $20 billion of US goods at rates reported between 15% and 50% across 700-plus tariff lines, TAKING EFFECT SEPTEMBER 8, 2026. Those figures are press-sourced (CNBC, Al Jazeera, NPR) rather than read from a government instrument, and are recorded as such. None of it touches the Section 301 forced-labour action or Canada's classification. The only "what we heard" report locatable on the ESDC and Global Affairs pages belongs to the earlier 2019/2022 consultation cycle, not this one -- a distinction worth holding onto, since a future run could easily mistake it for an outcome of the 2026 process. What Canada does with the responses is now the live question for this row, with no "what we heard" report, outcome or extension yet; the closing date was reconfirmed this run against Global Affairs Canada's own consultation page and a post by Foreign Minister Anita Anand. Bill C-35 re-verified again on August 19, 2026 by fetching the LegisInfo JSON directly, and the guard held exactly -- StatusNameEn still reads "At second reading in the House of Commons" while LatestBillEventTypeNameEn is "Introduction and first reading" dated 2026-06-12 and LatestCompletedMajorStageNameEn is "First reading": LatestBillEventTypeNameEn is still "Introduction and first reading" (June 12, 2026) and LatestCompletedMajorStageNameEn still "First reading" -- no second-reading debate, Parliament in summer recess. Canada also submitted written comments reiterating there is "no basis" for additional Section 301 duties. Canada stays Yes under the standing carve-out: an enacted ban in force is not downgraded by a separate pending strengthening bill. Re-checked September 2, 2026 against LegisInfo directly: Bill C-35's last completed stage is still first reading of June 12, 2026 -- the "at second reading" label denotes the stage awaited, not one reached -- and no second-reading debate has occurred, which is unsurprising since the House of Commons does not resume until September 21, 2026. The Global Affairs/CBSA/ESDC consultation that closed August 21 still has no "what we heard" report or outcome statement, twelve days on. Source: Parliament of Canada LegisInfo (primary, checked directly); Global Affairs Canada, June 12 and July 27, 2026. USTR's final determination of July 23, 2026 confirmed a 10% tariff for Canada.
Official Forced Labor Import Ban: Yes (existing ban since 2020; Bill C-35 introduced June 12, 2026 and still only at first reading -- its LegisInfo status label "At second reading" denotes the stage awaited, not one completed -- with the Global Affairs Canada/CBSA and ESDC consultations now CLOSED, having ended as scheduled on August 21, 2026 with no extension and no outcome report published)

Summary and Source: China's Ministry of Commerce called USTR's final action "typical unilateralism and protectionism" (July 27, 2026), noted that the US itself has not ratified ILO Forced Labour Convention No. 29, and pointed to China's own labour-law framework and its ratification of 28 ILO conventions. ESCALATION this run: after DHS added 43 Chinese companies to the UFLPA Entity List on July 31 (taking it from 144 to 187 entities, effective August 3, 2026, published as Federal Register notice 2026-15628), MOFCOM moved from verbal condemnation -- calling the listing "completely groundless" and "economic coercion" -- to ACTUAL COUNTERMEASURES on August 5, 2026: tightened export controls on drones, their key components and related technologies bound for the United States, which now face strict case-by-case review with license-facilitation measures withdrawn, plus suspension of part of China-US product-certification cooperation. No retaliatory tariff has been announced, and reporting attributes the restraint partly to a planned Xi-Trump summit. CLASSIFICATION UNCHANGED: these are retaliatory trade-control measures and the UFLPA listing is a US enforcement action -- neither is a Chinese forced-labour import prohibition, and Chinese-language searches continue to find no PRC import-ban law. Source: MOFCOM, July 27 and August 5, 2026; Global Times, August 1 and August 2026; US Department of Homeland Security, July 31, 2026; Federal Register 2026-15628.
Official Forced Labor Import Ban: No

Summary and Source: President Abinader issued Decreto num. 502-26 on July 23, 2026 -- the day the 12.5% US tariff took effect -- establishing an administrative procedure empowering the Direccion General de Aduanas (DGA), coordinated with the Labor Ministry, Public Ministry, Industry and Commerce and Foreign Affairs, to identify, restrict and prohibit importation of merchandise produced wholly or partly with forced labor. The decree creates a public registry of prohibited products and lets DGA preventively retain or bar suspect goods including consignments already in transit or sitting at port, with re-export or destruction as remedies. DATE DISCREPANCY RESOLVED this run: at least one secondary outlet (Revista Mercado) dates the decree to June 23, 2026; the Presidency's own decree page for 502-26 carries 23 de Julio 2026, so the July 23 date recorded here is confirmed against the primary source and the June date is incorrect. The private sector has raised implementation concerns and commentators question enforcement capacity; no implementing regulation has been issued and no enforcement action has yet been identified. Source: Presidencia de la Republica Dominicana (primary, decree page re-verified August 3, 2026); Diario Libre, July 23 and 26, 2026; El Nuevo Diario.
Official Forced Labor Import Ban: Yes (Decreto No. 502-26, issued July 23, 2026 -- date confirmed against the Presidency's own decree page; establishes a public registry of prohibited products and empowers customs (DGA) to preventively retain and bar forced-labor-linked merchandise, including goods already in transit or at port, with re-export or destruction as remedies)

Summary and Source: Ecuador holds the 10% tier on the basis of COMEX Resolution 005-2026, which created the inter-institutional technical team (ETITF, spanning the Production Ministry, customs authority SENAE and the Labour Ministry) to restrict imports of forced-labor-produced goods; USTR credits the measure but assesses enforcement as weak, and no enforcement action has been identified. Production Minister Luis Alberto Jaramillo reiterated at USA Trade Connect 2026 in Guayaquil (July 28) that Ecuador "complies with its commitments and controls." The separate US-Ecuador Reciprocal Trade Agreement signed March 13, 2026 is NOT yet in force -- it still requires Constitutional Court review and National Assembly approval -- and Ecuador has a 12-month window to stand up its compliance systems, so Ecuador's Yes rests on the enacted COMEX resolution, not the unratified RTA. SOURCING CORRECTION, August 19, 2026: column 6 had been pointing at the Ministry of Production's copy of the US-Ecuador RECIPROCAL TRADE AGREEMENT text -- by its own filename the RTA, not the ban instrument -- which is the wrong document to cite for a row whose Yes rests on the COMEX resolution. It has been repointed to the Ministry's own copy of Resolucion COMEX 005-2026. Stated honestly: that URL was fetched from here and returns HTTP 200 as a valid 12-page PDF on produccion.gob.ec, the competent ministry's own domain, with the resolution named in the filename, but this environment has no PDF text extractor and a raw stream decode surfaced no readable keywords, so the identification rests on host, filename and successful retrieval rather than on a reading of the text. DATE NUANCE, clarified: the resolution itself is dated April 2026 (the Ministry hosts it under a /2026/04/ path) and was published in the Registro Oficial on May 15, 2026; a research pass this run framed these as competing dates, but signature and gazette publication are simply different events. IMPLEMENTATION GAP, re-checked August 19, 2026: the ETITF's operational manual -- which the resolution gave a 90-day window to draft and which the mechanism needs before investigations can begin -- has still NOT been published, and that 90-day window has now expired on either the April or the May reckoning. No company list and no enforcement action has appeared. The mechanism remains formally enacted but operationally dormant, consistent with USTR's weak-enforcement assessment. Source: Ministerio de Produccion (Resolucion COMEX 005-2026, government-direct); El Universo and Primicias, July 2026.
Official Forced Labor Import Ban: Yes (COMEX Resolution 005-2026 establishing the inter-institutional ETITF mechanism restricting forced-labor-linked imports, dated April 2026 and published in the Registro Oficial May 15, 2026; USTR assesses enforcement as weak and the ETITF's operational manual remains unpublished with its 90-day drafting window now expired, so the mechanism is enacted but operationally dormant. The separate US-Ecuador RTA signed March 13, 2026 is not yet in force -- it still requires Constitutional Court review and National Assembly approval -- and is not the basis for this classification. Re-confirmed August 31, 2026: the ETITF operational manual is still unpublished)

Summary and Source: El Salvador's enacted domestic ban (Article 27-A customs-law reform, in force since March 2026) remains the operative basis for its 10% tariff tier. Separately, per Coexport (the exporters' association) and La Prensa Grafica, the US-El Salvador Agreement on Reciprocal Trade (signed January 29, 2026) is understood by the private sector to remain not yet in force -- El Salvador's tariff treatment rests on the enacted domestic law, not the RTA. Source: La Prensa Grafica, July 9, 2026; El Mundo/Coexport, July 2026. RTA ENTRY-INTO-FORCE MECHANISM NAMED, September 5, though the question stays open: USTR's own account of the agreement provides that it enters into force "five days after both parties exchange written notification that domestic procedures have been completed," contingent on Salvadoran congressional approval and a US Executive Order. No evidence of such an exchange was found, which corroborates without proving the sourced position that the January 29, 2026 RTA is not yet in force. An AI-generated summary asserting it has been "in force since January" remains unadopted. None of this affects the classification, which rests on the enacted Article 27-A customs-law reform rather than the RTA.
Official Forced Labor Import Ban: Yes (Article 27-A customs-law reform, in force since March 2026; the separate US-El Salvador RTA, signed January 29, 2026, remains not yet in force per private-sector reporting, but is not the basis for El Salvador's Yes classification)

Summary and Source: USTR credits the EU with an enacted prohibition but assesses enforcement as inadequate because Regulation (EU) 2024/3015 is not applicable until December 14, 2027. Article 3 verified directly from EUR-Lex: "Economic operators shall not place or make available on the Union market products that are made with forced labour, nor shall they export such products." The Regulation is marked "(Text with EEA relevance)," the basis for Norway's incorporation, and Article 2(1) defines forced labour by reference to ILO Convention No. 29. The Commission's implementation guidelines of June 26, 2026 (C(2026) 4386 final) and the Forced Labour Single Portal are confirmed on the Commission's own initiative page, with implementation-readiness webinars scheduled from September 2026. SCHEDULE CONFIRMED this run: the Commission's programme opens in September 2026 with a general introduction to the Forced Labour Regulation and its preparedness package, followed by SME-focused guidance sessions and sector-specific sessions running through November 2026, including a dedicated TEXTILE-sector workshop on October 20, 2026. All of this is readiness support for a prohibition that still does not apply until December 14, 2027, so the classification is unaffected. NEW this run and verified directly against EUR-Lex: Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2026/903 of 24 April 2026, adopted under Article 7(7)(a) of Reg. 2024/3015, specifies the details and functionalities of the information and communication system for the Regulation -- a dedicated forced-labour module within ICSMS (the market-surveillance system under Reg. (EU) 2019/1020), used for the general-provisions, investigations, decisions and enforcement chapters and for data exchange between the Commission, national competent authorities and customs. Its Article 11 provides that it enters into force on the twentieth day following publication in the Official Journal. THAT DATE IS NOW CONFIRMED FROM THE PRIMARY TEXT, retrieved directly from EUR-Lex this run: the implementing regulation is dated 24 April 2026 and its OJ citation is "OJ L, 2026/903, 27.4.2026," so the twentieth day following publication is 17 May 2026 -- which corroborates the date previously carried here only on secondary reporting. Its subject matter is also now stated precisely from the title: it specifies the details and functionalities of the information and communication system to be used for the purposes of Regulation (EU) 2024/3015. All of this is machinery for a still-inapplicable prohibition, so classification is unchanged. Source: EUR-Lex (primary texts of Reg. 2024/3015 and Implementing Reg. 2026/903); European Commission initiative 16292 and C(2026) 4386 final, June 26, 2026.
Official Forced Labor Import Ban: Yes (Regulation (EU) 2024/3015, Article 3 prohibition, in force but not applicable until December 14, 2027; Commission implementation guidelines adopted June 26, 2026, Forced Labour Single Portal live, and Implementing Reg. (EU) 2026/903 of 24 April 2026 establishing the ICSMS forced-labour module)

Summary and Source: Guatemala's Acuerdo Ministerial 377-2026 (published July 6, 2026) secured it the 10% tier. Classification is Yes and has never been in doubt: the instrument is formally published by the competent authority, which the standing policy treats as enactment even before effectiveness. THE LONGEST-RUNNING OPEN QUESTION IN THIS TRACKER -- the entry-into-force date -- IS NOW RESOLVED, AND CONFIRMED GOVERNMENT-SIDE. Prensa Libre, August 18, 2026 (18:24h, Rosa Maria Bolanos), retrieved and read directly this run, reports: "El 17 de agosto del 2026 entro en vigencia el Acuerdo Ministerial 377-2026, que prohibe en Guatemala las importaciones de bienes producidos mediante trabajo forzoso y obligatorio." It explains that the acuerdo was issued by the Ministerio de Economia (Mineco) jointly with the Ministerio de Trabajo y Prevision Social (Mintrab) and "establece que entra en vigencia 30 dias habiles despues de ser publicado en el diario oficial el 6 de julio ultimo," and -- decisively -- "AMBOS MINISTERIOS CONFIRMARON LA FECHA." That is confirmation from both competent ministries, far stronger than the outlet-characterisation evidence previously available, and it settles the 30-dias-HABILES reading against the 30-calendar-day reading. It also vindicates the AUGUST 16 CORRECTION recorded here, which reversed this row's August 12 framing: on August 12 this row had said the weight of evidence favoured a 30-CALENDAR-day count (~August 5, already in force), resting on the Diario de Centro America's parenthetical gloss of vigencia as "30 dias posteriores a la publicacion" with no "habiles" qualifier. That over-weighted a parenthetical; La Hora's same-day July 6 report ("la vigencia del Acuerdo sera efectiva dentro de 30 dias HABILES a partir de este 6 de julio") was the basis for the reversal, and 30 business days from July 6 lands exactly on Monday August 17, 2026. NEXT DEADLINE, NOW HARD-DATED: Mintrab has 90 dias calendario from entry into force to prepare and publish the Listado Oficial of foreign companies linked to forced labour, "plazo que, segun esa institucion, se cumple el 15 DE NOVIEMBRE proximo," and the publication must be made on the Mineco and Mintrab websites; to compile it Mintrab may use information obtained through diplomatic channels and other international sources. Economy Minister Gabriela Garcia said on Tuesday August 18 that Mintrab has asked the Ministerio de Relaciones Exteriores (Minex) to request the list of companies through diplomatic channels. Article 4 of the acuerdo carries the prohibition itself: "Se prohibe la importacion de bienes extranjeros extraidos, producidos o manufacturados total o parcialmente mediante trabajo forzoso u obligatorio." NEW THIS RUN, retrieved and read directly: a further Prensa Libre report ("Importaciones en Guatemala: expertos advierten riesgos por acuerdo sobre trabajo forzoso") sets out the implementation mechanics and the criticism of them. Mintrab is to compile the Listado Oficial by requesting information "por conducto diplomatico," updating it annually or when circumstances change, and MINECO is the body that transmits the list to the customs authority for the corresponding controls -- so SAT acts only once it receives the list, and no SAT implementing circular has been published. Ruben Morales, a former Economy Minister and foreign-trade specialist, and the other experts interviewed say the acuerdo's provisions are very broad, that it sets out no methodology for identifying goods linked to forced labour and provides for no independent Guatemalan investigation, leaving it dependent on foreign lists, and that it requires coordination between Mineco, Mintrab and SAT that is not clearly specified. These are implementation risks, not classification questions: the instrument is enacted and in force. Source: Prensa Libre, August 18 and August 2026; La Hora, July 6, 2026; Diario de Centro America (official gazette outlet), July 2026.
Official Forced Labor Import Ban: Yes (Acuerdo Ministerial 377-2026, published July 6, 2026, article 4 prohibiting importation of goods produced wholly or partly with forced or compulsory labour regardless of origin; ENTRY INTO FORCE CONFIRMED as MONDAY AUGUST 17, 2026 -- Prensa Libre, August 18, 2026 reports the acuerdo "entro en vigencia" that day on the 30-dias-habiles count and states that both competent ministries, Mineco and Mintrab, confirmed the date, which settles the question and vindicates this row's August 16 correction of its August 12 calendar-day framing. Mintrab's company-specific Listado Oficial is due 90 calendar days after vigencia, a deadline Mintrab itself puts at NOVEMBER 15, 2026, for publication on the Mineco and Mintrab websites; Economy Minister Gabriela Garcia said on August 18 that Mintrab has asked Minex to request the company list through diplomatic channels)

Summary and Source: Guyana's Ministry of Labour (represented by Sharon Roopchand-Edwards) testified at the July 7 USTR hearing, stating Guyana is "not aware of evidence" that forced-labor goods are made in, imported into, or exported from Guyana, citing constitutional protections, the Combating of Trafficking in Persons Act, ILO Convention 29/105 ratification, and Customs Act authority to block goods with credible evidence of forced labor; Guyana urged reconsideration of the proposed tariff and noted ongoing bilateral trade-agreement talks with the US. Source: Official USTR hearing transcript, Day 1, July 7, 2026. It is a defence/security arrangement -- a Guyana Defence Force / State Department liaison-officer memorandum -- not a trade agreement, and it carries no forced-labour or import-prohibition clause. It therefore does NOT place Guyana on the RTA-commitment watchlist. USTR issued its FINAL Section 301 forced-labor determination on July 23, 2026 (Ambassador Greer, per direction of the President), confirming a final tariff of 12.5% for Guyana, timed to replace the expiring Section 122 10% global surcharge. Summary and Source: Honduras testified at the July 7 USTR hearing (Melvin Redondo, Presidential Office of Foreign Trade), announcing an executive decree creating an express prohibition on importing forced-labour-made goods, and requested a 10% "bridge rate." The Council of Ministers approved the decree on the night of July 16, 2026; it was published the next day as Decreto Ejecutivo No. PCM-014-2026 in La Gaceta No. 37,196 (July 17, 2026), citing ILO Conventions 29/105 and CAFTA-DR obligations. Article 4 prohibits importing goods produced wholly or partly with forced/compulsory labour, effective on publication, and Article 7 directs Customs to build the prohibited-goods list into its risk-management system, with intercepted goods facing re-export or destruction at importer cost. THE IMPLEMENTING LIST HAS NOW BEEN PUBLISHED, AND THIS ROW CORRECTS A SUSTAINED ERROR OF ITS OWN. Acuerdo Ministerial No. SETRASS-527-2026 -- "Regulacion para la implementacion del Decreto Ejecutivo PCM-014-2026 y aprobacion de la Lista de Mercancias con Prohibicion de Importacion, Primera Edicion 2026" -- was published as item 1 of La Gaceta Edition No. 37,226 of AUGUST 21, 2026, signed by Labour Secretary Fernando Puerto Castro. I read the full text directly. Article 32 puts the Acuerdo in force on the day of publication; Article 28 approves the Annex I list "integrada por seis registros"; and Article 29 defers the prohibition itself, so it "empezara a implementarse treinta dias calendario despues de la publicacion" -- i.e. ENFORCEMENT BEGINS SEPTEMBER 20, 2026. HOW THE LIST WAS BUILT, which is the substantively interesting part: the Permanent Technical Commission reported on August 14 that ILO, UN Special Rapporteur, Walk Free and US Department of Labor reports establish forced-labour practices in given countries or sectors but do NOT identify a specific producer or supply chain, so listing countries or regions from them would assume all their goods are tainted and create discrimination and trade barriers contrary to Article 6 of the decree. The Commission therefore built the First Edition EXCLUSIVELY from homologated US CBP Final Determinations (Findings), expressly excluding Withhold Release Orders as resting only on reasonable suspicion. It also declined to adopt the Xinjiang (UFLPA) entity list, reasoning that it was issued by an authority other than the customs authority and so is not shown to be equivalent under Article 3(e) -- left open for later editions. Article 14 forbids listings by tariff chapter, sector, country or region without an identified producer, and goods from prison establishments require extra analysis against the ILO C29 Article 2(2)(c) penal-labour exception. The six Annex I registros are five Chinese producers plus one fishing vessel: the Da Wang (operated by Yong Feng Fishery Ltd, Vanuatu-Taiwan, 87 FR 4634); Inner Mongolia Hengzheng Group Baoanzhao Agriculture, Industry and Trade (stevia extracts, 85 FR 66574); Tianjin Malleable Iron Factory a.k.a. Tianjin No. 2 prison (malleable iron pipe fittings, 61 FR 17956); Qinghai Hide & Garment Factory (sheepskins and leather); and two further Chinese producers. HS references are indicative only until Honduran Customs fixes the exact CAI classification under Article 15. The Honduran Chamber of Commerce and Industry (CCIT) has been warning importers that non-compliance could see goods blocked at the border. Source: Official USTR hearing transcript, Day 1, July 7, 2026; La Gaceta No. 37,196 of July 17, 2026 and No. 37,226 of August 21, 2026, both read directly via leyes.hn; Hondudiario and Proceso Digital, August 2026. USTR's final determination of July 23, 2026 confirmed a 10% tariff for Honduras.
Official Forced Labor Import Ban: Yes (Decreto Ejecutivo PCM-014-2026, La Gaceta No. 37,196, July 17, 2026, effective on publication; the implementing instrument and prohibited-goods list are NOW PUBLISHED -- Acuerdo Ministerial SETRASS-527-2026 in La Gaceta Edition No. 37,226 of August 21, 2026, in force on publication under its Article 32, with the import prohibition on the six Annex I registros deferred 30 calendar days under Article 29 so that ENFORCEMENT BEGINS SEPTEMBER 20, 2026. CORRECTION OF THIS ROW'S OWN REPORTING, recorded plainly rather than quietly overwritten: for nine consecutive runs from August 21 to August 29 this row asserted that the STSS list had not been published, and that was WRONG throughout. The list was published on August 21 in Edition 37,226 -- the very edition this row kept naming as the unchanged index ceiling. The error was methodological and is worth stating precisely: I read only the gazette INDEX, which lists edition numbers, dates and item counts, and I searched that index for "forzoso"/"STSS", which do not appear in index metadata. I never fetched the contents of Edition 37,226 itself. The "34 items" I repeatedly recorded for that edition included the Acuerdo as item 1. Every downstream inference built on the absence -- the "seven-day gazette freeze" narrative, the claim that the freeze breaking made the negative "materially stronger," and the conclusion that "the delay is not a publishing outage, it is the list itself not being ready" -- was therefore false, and is withdrawn in full. The lesson is the same one this tracker already learned for Honduras and Vietnam in a different form: an index is not the document, and a negative drawn from a summary view is not a negative drawn from the text. Gazette re-read on August 30: ceiling now Edition No. 37,233 of August 29, 2026, with 37,231 (Aug 27, 46 items), 37,232 (Aug 28, 56 items) and 37,233 (Aug 29, 6 items) all new since the last run and each fetched IN FULL this time -- none contains further forced-labour content; the only SETRASS hits in 37,232 are two copies of an unrelated administrative lawsuit over a personnel cancellation. Re-read again on August 31: the index ceiling is UNCHANGED at Edition No. 37,233 of August 29, with no new edition over the weekend, which is expected rather than notable since August 30 was a Sunday. No customs or OPCE Article 15 tariff-classification determination for the six registros has been published, no second edition or addition to the Annex I list has appeared, and no reaction from China or the listed producers has been found. Re-read again on September 1 and September 2: the ceiling is still Edition No. 37,233 of August 29, with no September edition yet and enforcement now EIGHTEEN days out. A research pass also checked the Chinese embassy in Tegucigalpa's own news index and Spanish-language sources and found NO reaction from China, the embassy or the listed producers to Honduras having named five Chinese firms -- a silence worth recording given what was listed. On the earlier reading, the ceiling was still Edition No. 37,233 of August 29 -- no September edition has appeared yet -- with zero occurrences of "forzoso" in the index, and still no customs or OPCE Article 15 tariff-classification determination, no second edition of the Annex I list, and no reaction found from China or the listed producers. THE GAZETTE HAS MOVED AGAIN AND BOTH NEW EDITIONS WERE OPENED, NOT JUST COUNTED -- the distinction that cost this row nine runs. As of September 3 the ceiling is Edition No. 37,235 of September 1, 2026 (97 items), with Edition No. 37,234 of August 31 (83 items) also new. A research pass opened 37,235 and found only a Roatan Electric tariff adjustment, municipal bidding notices, an administrative-court filing and trademark notices, but did NOT open 37,234; I fetched 37,234 myself to close that gap. It contains zero occurrences of "forzoso", zero "STSS" and no OPCE item, and its two SETRASS hits and sixteen "aduana" hits were each read and are all benign: the SETRASS references are an unrelated 2025 personnel lawsuit over Acuerdo No. SETRASS-272-2025, and the customs references are a HONDUCOR petty-cash regulation setting departmental cash limits plus a trademark filing listing customs-brokerage services. So neither new edition carries the Article 15 classification, a second edition of the list, or any addition to it. Still no reaction from China, the Chinese embassy in Tegucigalpa (whose own news index was checked) or the listed producers -- a continuing silence worth recording given five Chinese firms were named. Re-read September 4: the ceiling has advanced again to Edition No. 37,236 of September 2, 2026 (39 items), whose CONTENTS were opened rather than counted -- Decreto Ejecutivo No. 024-2026 reorganising the Infrastructure/Transport ministry, a grain-inventory notice, two frequency-plan resolutions, lawsuits, an edicto and trademarks, with zero occurrences of "forzoso", STSS, SETRASS, aduana or OPCE. What to watch now is no longer publication but ENFORCEMENT from September 20 -- SIXTEEN days out -- and the Article 15 customs classification, which remains the conspicuous missing piece: without it the six registros carry only indicative HS references, and no determination has appeared anywhere. September 5: the ceiling has advanced to Edition No. 37,237 of September 3, 2026 (58 items), whose CONTENTS were opened -- DIGER cybersecurity contracting and delegation agreements, a PRONADERS agreement, legal notices, property titles and trademarks, with zero "forzoso", STSS, SETRASS, aduana or OPCE. On the Article 15 point the status is now honestly WEAKER than "absent": aduanas.gob.hn returned HTTP 403 to a research pass and to me on both www and bare-domain forms, so its absence is unverified rather than confirmed. FIRST CONCRETE EVIDENCE OF PREPARATION, fifteen days out: the Tegucigalpa Chamber of Commerce (CCIT) is actively advising importers to strengthen due diligence, establish the origin of imported products, request supplier information on labour practices and maintain supply-chain traceability, and is offering technical and legal assistance to help importers adjust their commercial files before the prohibition bites. That is the first sign this row has seen of the private sector actually preparing, as opposed to the instrument merely existing. September 6, fourteen days out: the gazette ceiling is UNCHANGED at Edition No. 37,237 of September 3, so there was nothing newer to open. aduanas.gob.hn returned HTTP 403 again -- to a research pass and to me -- and alternate routes via OPCE, SAR and gob.hn portals surfaced nothing, so the Article 15 classification remains UNVERIFIED rather than confirmed absent, which is the honest characterisation and has now held for three days. No further preparation signs beyond the CCIT advisory, and still no reaction from China, the Tegucigalpa embassy or the listed producers. Independent corroboration of the substance from ICN Digital and La Prensa, which confirm the September 20 date and the six-registro breakdown and describe the vessel operator as a Taiwan company -- consistent with, not contradicting, the Vanuatu-Taiwan detail already recorded. Summary and Source: DGFT Notification No. 23/2026-27, dated 13 July 2026, was verified directly against the primary document (an image-only scanned PDF, rendered and read visually after text extraction failed on every earlier attempt). Verified from the document: headed "To be published in the Gazette of India Extraordinary Part-II, Section-3, Sub-Section (ii)," issued under Section 3 read with Section 5 of the Foreign Trade (Development & Regulation) Act, 1992 and paras 1.02 and 2.01 of FTP 2023, signed by Lav Agarwal, Director General of Foreign Trade, File No. K-31013/1/2026-DIR NAFTA-Part(4). New Para 2.20B: "The import of goods produced or manufactured, wholly or in part, through the use of forced labour is prohibited. The Central Government may, from time to time, specify, by notification, the goods whose import shall be prohibited under this paragraph... The procedure for conducting an enquiry by the Director General of Foreign Trade into the use of forced labour in the production of such goods shall be as prescribed in the Handbook of Procedures, 2023." New Para 11.64 defines "Forced Labour" per ILO Convention No. 29. The first sentence is a flat self-executing prohibition; the notification power goes to designating specific goods, structurally like Trinidad and Tobago's ban. EFFECTIVE DATE, still an inference: the text ties effect to "the expiry of 30 days from the date of publication of this Notification in the Official Gazette," and no source -- egazette.gov.in, PIB or press -- states a Gazette publication date distinct from DGFT's own notification date (13/07/2026) and portal posting (14/07/2026). The widely cited ~12 August 2026 date follows from assuming those coincide and is recorded as an inference, not a verified figure. THE INFERRED EFFECTIVE DATE PASSED ON AUGUST 12, 2026 AND NOTHING CONFIRMS IT: as of August 19, seven days past the inferred date, no source reports that the prohibition has taken effect, and the Gazette publication date remains unstated everywhere checked (egazette.gov.in, PIB, Indian press, Hindi-language search). The tracker therefore does NOT record the ban as in force -- only as enacted with an unverified effective date. NO DESIGNATED GOODS AS OF AUGUST 19, 2026, re-checked directly against DGFT's own notification index rather than news: the index still runs through No. 28/2026-27 dated 5 August 2026 (e-commerce export framework, halal certification, export-policy harmonisation, PVC resin, ITC(HS) syncing), and No. 23/2026-27 -- listed there as "Prohibition on Import of Goods Produced Using Forced Labour -- Insertion of Para 2.20B and Para 11.64 in the Foreign Trade Policy (FTP) 2023," notification date 13/07/2026 -- remains the ONLY forced-labour notification. No banned-goods list, trade notice or Handbook of Procedures amendment has been issued under Para 2.20B. Source: DGFT Notification No. 23/2026-27 (primary document); DGFT notification index, dgft.gov.in (checked directly August 10, 2026); corroborated by Taxscan, Business Today, The Wire and an ELP legal alert.

Summary and Source: MATERIAL ADVANCE THIS RUN, VERIFIED AGAINST THE HEBREW SOURCE DIRECTLY: the KNESSET ECONOMIC COMMITTEE (Va'adat HaKalkala) has UNANIMOUSLY APPROVED the order banning imports of goods made with forced labour. JDN's report, read directly in Hebrew, states: "Va'adat HaKalkala shel HaKnesset ishra hayom (hamishi) pe echad tzav histori ha'oser larishona al yevu mutzarim she'yutzru be'avodat kfiya" -- the Knesset Economic Committee approved today (Thursday), unanimously, a historic order prohibiting for the first time the import of products produced with forced labour. DATE PINNED DOWN HERE, which the research pass could not do: the article says "today (Thursday)" and carries the Hebrew date byline 30 Av, and 30 Av 5786 corresponds to THURSDAY, AUGUST 13, 2026 -- the weekday and the Hebrew date agree, so the committee approval is dated August 13, 2026. The order was initiated by the Ministry of Economy following staff work coordinated by Prof. Avi Simhon of the National Economic Council, and the report is explicit that it was taken under the shadow of the US tariff, framed as aligning Israel with international standards and enabling an approach to Washington to reduce the tariff on Israeli exports to 10%. STRUCTURE, which is why this is not yet Yes: the order is expressly a framework -- "a foundational legal infrastructure" that will now ALLOW concrete products to be added to the prohibited-import list. Every future addition of specific products will require FRESH approval of the Economic Committee, accompanied by scrutiny of objection and appeal mechanisms and by adequate preparation periods for importers before any prohibition takes effect. So no product is banned yet, and no signed ministerial order or Reshumot (official gazette) entry has been reported. CLASSIFICATION STAYS PARTIAL on that basis -- committee approval of an order is a decisive step but not yet an issued instrument. FORWARD-LOOKING NOTE for future runs: once the order is signed and published in Reshumot, Israel should move to YES even with an empty product schedule, on the same reasoning that treats Trinidad and Tobago's Customs Act s.45(1)(w) and India's FTP Para 2.20B as Yes despite their designation-dependent structure. This supersedes the prior position that the implementing order was merely pending with an inter-ministerial task force still designing the mechanism. The Cabinet decision of July 26, 2026 (Hebrew sources Walla and Davar) remains the origin of the process, and follow-up Hebrew searching this run corroborates that it set an explicit 90-DAY implementation window -- directing Economy Minister Nir Barkat to stand up the order together with its mechanism design, appeals and reporting arrangements -- which places the outer deadline around late October 2026 and is consistent with the August 13 committee approval landing well inside it. Re-checked August 19, 2026 in Hebrew: still no signed ministerial order and no Reshumot entry, six days after the committee approval. FALSE-DATE GUARD, still standing: a claim that the decision was "approved February 22, 2026" has surfaced on numerous runs and has never been corroborated in any language; it is not adopted. Source: JDN (Hebrew), August 13, 2026, read directly; Emess (Hebrew); Walla and Davar (Hebrew), July 2026.

Summary and Source: Japan submitted a written comment citing its July 2025 bilateral trade agreement with the US and asking for "appropriate actions" (implicit request for tariff relief); Japan did not testify live at the July 7-9 hearings. NEW CONTEXT THIS RUN, not enough to change the classification: an LDP lawmaker has floated drafting a Japanese UFLPA-style forced-labour import law, and Human Rights Watch has publicly urged Japan to adopt such a regulation. Both are proposals and advocacy -- no bill has been tabled in the Diet -- so Japan stays No under the standing policy, which requires at least a formally tabled or published measure for Partial. Source: International Economic Law and Policy Blog, July 2026; Human Rights Watch, February 2026. USTR issued its FINAL Section 301 forced-labor determination on July 23, 2026 (Ambassador Greer, per direction of the President), confirming a final tariff of 12.5% (net of MFN) for Japan, timed to replace the expiring Section 122 10% global surcharge. OPEN QUESTION RAISED THIS RUN, from the primary text and NOT acted on: the companion Presidential Document (Federal Register doc 2026-15274), which I retrieved and read directly, states that "for goods of the European Union, Japan, Korea, Switzerland, or Taiwan, section 301 tariffs that are the net of Most-Favored Nation (MFN) tariffs would be consistent with their respective Agreements on Reciprocal Trade or similar arrangements and would be appropriate to encourage these economies to fulfill commitments regarding forced labor imports." That sentence groups this economy with Taiwan, whose Partial classification rests precisely on an RTA forced-labour commitment, and its phrase "commitments regarding forced labor imports" could be read as implying one exists here too. It is NOT being treated as establishing one: the sentence is about how the tariff is calculated (netting against MFN) and about encouragement, the tariff outcome here is the 12.5% top-up rather than the 10% tier given to commitment economies, and no agreement text containing a forced-labour import-prohibition clause has been located. SETTLED THIS RUN, AND THE ANSWER IS NO. The only US-Japan instrument in force is the 2025 framework agreement announced July 22, 2025 and implemented by Executive Order 14345 of September 4, 2025 with Federal Register notices 2025-17389 and 2025-17908. Its substantive terms cover a 15% baseline tariff, sectoral carve-outs for autos, aerospace, pharmaceuticals and natural resources, Japanese purchase commitments on agricultural goods, energy and aircraft, an investment facility, and recognition of US auto standards -- and contain NO forced-labour, Section 307 or import-prohibition clause. No separate 2026 US-Japan Agreement on Reciprocal Trade exists, and Japan does not appear among the economies whose ARTs carry forced-labour commitments. The Presidential Document's "commitments regarding forced labor imports" phrasing is therefore encouraging or aspirational language in Japan's case, not a reference to an existing treaty clause. Japan stays No, and this question should not be reopened without new evidence of an actual instrument. Source: USTR press release and White House presidential action, July 23, 2026; Federal Register doc 2026-15274 (primary text).
Official Forced Labor Import Ban: No

Summary and Source: The U.S.-Jordan Agreement on Reciprocal Trade, signed July 21, 2026, commits Jordan under Article 2.9(1) -- text directly verified -- to prohibit importation of goods mined, produced or manufactured wholly or in part by forced or compulsory labor within five years of entry into force, and to recognize and presumptively enforce US Section 307 Withhold Release Order determinations. RESOLVED this run: the 10% tariff figure, previously carried as sourced only to Law360 and unverified against the agreement's Annex I, is now confirmed from the primary US source -- USTR's Federal Register notice (doc 2026-15181, published July 28, 2026) states the Trade Representative determined, "including consideration of Jordan's commitment in its ART related to prohibiting the importation of forced labor goods," to "impose 10 percent tariffs on products of Jordan, except as provided in Annex I and Annex II, Parts A, N, and O." The bilateral agreement's own Annex I still could not be retrieved, but it is no longer load-bearing for the rate; Arab News independently corroborates the 10% cap. No domestic Jordanian ban has been enacted. Source: White House agreement text; Federal Register doc 2026-15181, July 28, 2026; Arab News, July 2026.
Official Forced Labor Import Ban: Partial (U.S.-Jordan Agreement on Reciprocal Trade, signed July 21, 2026, Art. 2.9(1), directly verified: Jordan commits to prohibit forced-labor imports within 5 years of entry into force; no domestic implementing law enacted yet. The 10% US tariff rate is NOW VERIFIED from the primary Federal Register notice, which ties it expressly to Jordan's ART forced-labor commitment. AN ENTRY-INTO-FORCE CLAIM IS CIRCULATING AND IS NOT ADOPTED -- it has now surfaced twice, on September 3 and again on September 5, in Arabic-language reporting asserting the ART 'entered into force on August 1, 2026'. This MATTERS more than an ordinary date, because Article 2.9(1) runs Jordan's five-year clock to prohibit forced-labour imports FROM entry into force: if August 1 is right, the obligation matures on 1 August 2031. A research pass tried to fetch the CNN Arabic source for the exact sentence and got HTTP 451 (Unavailable for Legal Reasons), so no quotable primary or accessible text supports it yet. The date is therefore recorded as a live but UNVERIFIED claim, to be adopted only against an official source -- the same standard that caught the Peruvian expediente number and the Mexican March date. SEPTEMBER 6: THE CLAIM STRENGTHENED WITHOUT MEETING THE STANDARD, and both halves of that matter. It has now surfaced a THIRD time and, for the first time, in quotable form: a CNN Arabic headline of August 7, 2026 reads "دخلت حيز التنفيذ.. ما مكاسب اتفاقية التجارة الجديدة بين الأردن وأمريكا؟" ("[It] entered into force -- what are the gains of the new Jordan-America trade agreement?"), and a separate Arabic report states flatly "دخلت اتفاقية التجارة المتبادلة الجديدة بين الأردن والولايات المتحدة الأمريكية حيز التنفيذ في الأول من أغسطس 2026." So this is no longer one outlet repeating itself; it is consistent across Arabic coverage. AGAINST THAT: I searched for a US-side instrument myself and there is none -- a Federal Register query for Jordan reciprocal-trade documents since July 1 returns only the two July 28 Section 301 items already on file and two wholly unrelated rules. I also fetched mit.gov.jo and petra.gov.jo directly; both loaded but carry no entry-into-force text (they are current-news homepages, and August 1 is five weeks back), and USTR's Jordan country page 404s. The honest position: three independent Arabic reports now say August 1, no official or primary source has been reached to confirm it, and the tracker does not adopt it. If it is right, Article 2.9(1)'s five-year clock matures on 1 August 2031 -- which is why this is worth chasing rather than shrugging at. SEPTEMBER 7: a FOURTH Arabic outlet now carries it -- jo24.net, almamlakatv.com, akhbarna.net and skynewsarabia.com all describe the agreement and its terms -- and the official route was tried properly this time and came up empty: searches for the Jordanian Official Gazette (الجريدة الرسمية) and for a Council of Ministers ratification decision returned nothing quoting a gazette publication or ratification date, and no mit.gov.jo, petra.gov.jo or Gazette page confirming entry into force could be reached. So the position hardens on both sides: the press claim is now consistent across four outlets, and the official record still cannot be made to confirm it. Not adopted. The distinction being preserved is between a widely repeated claim and a verified one, which is exactly the distinction that caught the Peruvian expediente number and the Mexican March date)

Summary and Source: Malaysia's 10% tier rests on its US Agreement on Reciprocal Trade (signed October 2025), which Minister Johari Abdul Ghani confirmed on July 25, 2026 is signed but not ratified -- the 2-year clock to legislate a forced-labour import ban starts only on ratification. Malay-language sources (Utusan Malaysia, RTM) add that Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim has said the US has not yet submitted a tariff proposal for ratification, so the matter remains pending on the US side as well. The earlier "null and void" episode followed the February 20, 2026 US Supreme Court ruling striking down IEEPA-based reciprocal tariffs and has since been superseded; that ruling does not disturb this action, since USTR's Federal Register notice rests solely on Sections 301(b) and 304(a) of the Trade Act of 1974 and never invokes IEEPA (verified directly against the notice). No forced-labour import-ban bill has been tabled. NEW THIS RUN, and it supplies the missing REASON for the ratification delay rather than just restating it: Malay-language reporting (Kosmo, Utusan) and a statement from Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim indicate the ART remains unratified because WASHINGTON has not yet submitted its tariff proposal for ratification -- so the hold-up is on the US side of the process, not Malaysian legislative reluctance. That matters for forecasting this row: the two-year clock cannot start until that step happens, so Malaysia is unlikely to move off Partial in the near term for reasons outside its own control. Source: Malay Mail and New Straits Times, July 25, 2026; Kosmo and Utusan Malaysia, June 2026; Utusan Malaysia and RTM; Federal Register doc 2026-15181.
Official Forced Labor Import Ban: Partial (US-Malaysia Agreement on Reciprocal Trade signed October 2025, still NOT ratified as of August 24, 2026, reportedly because the US has not yet submitted its tariff proposal for ratification; the 2-year clock to enact a domestic forced-labour import ban begins only on ratification, and no domestic bill has been tabled)

Summary and Source: Mexico's forced-labor import ban derives from a Ministry of Economy regulation implementing USMCA Article 23.6, published in the Diario Oficial de la Federacion on February 17, 2023 and effective May 2023, administered with the Labour Ministry (STPS); USTR credits it but assesses enforcement as weak, placing Mexico in the 10% tier. The 45-day consultation on non-USMCA-covered trade has concluded, with Economy Minister Ebrard confirming the 10% Section 301 rate substitutes for, rather than stacks on, the expired Section 122 surcharge, leaving Mexico's effective burden unchanged; USMCA-compliant goods (~85% of exports) remain exempt. Flagged for the tracker but OUTSIDE its scope: Ebrard has warned of a separate pending Section 301 "excess manufacturing capacity" investigation covering 16 economies that could bring fresh tariffs as early as August 2026 -- unrelated to forced labor and not tracked here. NEW this run, relevant to the enforcement weakness USTR relied on: per ProDESC, the Tribunal Federal de Justicia Administrativa (TFJA) agreed in March 2026 to hear a challenge to the STPS's dismissal of a forced-labour import-restriction request (the Empower petition), the first case to test the regulation's enforcement in court; a decision is still pending -- re-checked August 22, 2026 against the TFJA's own August bulletin, which covers an unrelated matter and carries no update on the case. DATE PINNED DOWN this run against ProDESC's own account, which earlier runs had left loose as "March" and then "March-May": ProDESC announced on MAY 18, 2026 that the TFJA had exercised its power to take up ("atraer") the case, the first time a Mexican tribunal has done so on forced-labour-linked imports. The underlying petition concerns Chinese-made surveillance cameras (Dahua/Hikvision) procured by Ciudad Juarez. Re-checked September 2, 2026: the TFJA has still issued NO ruling and the case remains pending. DATE DISCREPANCY RAISED AND RESOLVED IN FAVOUR OF THE EXISTING RECORD: two research passes this run reported the TFJA took the case up in "March 2026," which would contradict the May 18 date this row pinned down on August 27. I checked ProDESC's own news listing directly and it is dated "18 May" and reads "TFJA atrae por primera vez en Mexico caso sobre importaciones vinculadas con trabajo forzoso en China," with the item itself datelined "Ciudad de Mexico, 18 de mayo de 2026." The May 18, 2026 date therefore stands, verified at the primary source, and the March figure is rejected. Recorded because it was the second time a research pass had offered March. SETTLED ON SEPTEMBER 5: a pass fetched ProDESC's article directly and confirmed the May 18, 2026 date for a third time, quoting the tribunal's reasoning that it took the case up "considering it has special significance due to its implications in human rights, international trade, and labor obligations derived from the T-MEC," and confirming no ruling has issued -- "un tribunal tendra que decidir si eso es legal." The March figure is now treated as settled-wrong and should not be re-litigated. It does not affect the classification, which rests on the enacted 2023 regulation. Source: Diario Oficial de la Federacion, February 17, 2023; Mexico Business News, July 2026; ProDESC, 2026.
Official Forced Labor Import Ban: Yes (Ministry of Economy regulation implementing USMCA Article 23.6, published in the Diario Oficial February 17, 2023, effective May 2023; USTR assesses enforcement as weak)

Summary and Source: Morocco participated in confidential consultations with USTR, but "the consultations did not alter the outcome"; Morocco was found to lack a qualifying import ban and also filed formal written comments ahead of the July 7 hearing. ELECTION DATE RESOLVED: NOVEMBER 7, 2026, and the October 1 figure this row carried for many runs was WRONG. Convergent reporting from NZ Herald, RNZ, interest.co.nz and ABC News all attributes the date to Prime Minister Christopher Luxon's own announcement, and beehive.govt.nz carries a release titled "General Election to be held on 7 November." One honest limit: neither I nor the research pass could load the body text of that official release -- it returns an empty stub -- so the date rests on multiple independent secondary reports that each cite the announcement, not on a primary text I have read. REPORT-BACK HAPPENED ON SCHEDULE: on August 31, 2026 the Education and Workforce Select Committee recommended the bill be passed into law, with a NZ$100m revenue reporting threshold and no import-prohibition amendment, so the measure that emerged from committee is the same disclosure regime that went in. Source: RNZ and Interest.co.nz, July 2026 and RNZ, August 31, 2026; MFAT; DLA Piper; Transparency International NZ.
Official Forced Labor Import Ban: No (Modern Slavery Bill is a disclosure regime, not an import prohibition; still in select committee, with the select committee having REPORTED BACK ON TIME. Yesterday's sourcing gap is now closed: the Education and Workforce Select Committee recommended on Monday, August 31, 2026 -- the deadline itself -- that the Modern Slavery Bill be passed into law. No extension was needed. THE CLASSIFICATION IS UNCHANGED AT NO, because what was reported back is still a disclosure regime: the bill requires firms with revenue over NZ$100 million a year to report on their supply chains and operations, and NO import-prohibition amendment was recommended. I read the RNZ report directly and the page contains ZERO occurrences of the word "import." The bill is sponsored jointly by National MP Greg Fleming and Labour MP Camilla Belich, had support from all parties except ACT, and is the first bill introduced under Standing Order 288, which lets a member's bill bypass the ballot. Residual limit worth stating: this rests on RNZ rather than on the committee's own report or an Order Paper entry. SEPTEMBER 6 -- EVERY ROUTE TRIED AND DOCUMENTED, because after many runs of saying 'unreachable' it is worth recording precisely HOW each one fails: parliament.nz's bill page returned HTTP 200 but served a Radware bot-check screen with an incident ID and no legislative content; bills.parliament.nz's tracker URL loaded only nav chrome and 'An unhandled error has occurred', being a JavaScript app the fetcher cannot render; legislation.govt.nz returned HTTP 403 (a different failure from the empty HTTP 202 seen earlier, so the block is not even stable); and RNZ itself 403s to direct fetch, so even the secondary source is only reachable through search snippets. ONE ROUTE DID SERVE REAL CONTENT AND IS INSTRUCTIVE: the older server-rendered www3.parliament.nz subdomain loaded a genuine select-committee page -- but the MAY 2026 submissions-call page, with a 28 May closing date, predating the August 31 report-back entirely. A page that loads is not the same as a page that is current. No second reading has been scheduled or held on any account. SEPTEMBER 7 BROUGHT THE STRONGEST EVIDENCE THIS ROW HAS EVER HAD, and it is worth setting out because until now everything rested on one RNZ article reachable only through search snippets. A Bell Gully client note of September 1, 2026 sets out the select committee's ACTUAL recommended amendments in detail, and every one is disclosure-regime mechanics: the NZ$100 million threshold now measured over two preceding accounting periods; group and joint reporting; balance-date alignment; an approximately 24-month transition; substitution of an Australian modern-slavery statement for dual reporters; a new false-statement offence carrying up to NZ$200,000; pecuniary penalties up to NZ$600,000; and narrowed personal liability. Bell Gully states explicitly that there is NO mention of any import restriction or prohibition. That is a detailed positive account of what the committee actually changed, rather than an inference from silence, and it settles the question for this stage: what came out of committee is a transparency statute with teeth, not an import ban. A Daily Kos item of September 6 says the bill "is now heading toward a second reading" but gives no date. The classification is unchanged at No and now rests on far better sourcing, though still tier (b) -- the primary parliamentary record remains unreachable, and the www3.parliament.nz bill-tracker page returned HTTP 500 this run, a fourth distinct failure mode after the bot-check, the unrendered JavaScript app and the 403)

Summary and Source: Norway's government decided on July 21, 2026 to ban the import, export and sale of goods made with forced labour by incorporating EU Regulation 2024/3015 into the EEA Agreement, with Minister Cecilie Myrseth quoted: "Tvangsarbeid er selvfolgelig forbudt i Norge i dag, og gjennom dette regelverket innforer vi ogsa et forbud mot import av varer fremstilt ved tvangsarbeid." Re-checked in Norwegian on August 19, 2026 against both regjeringen.no and stortinget.no: regjeringen.no now states explicitly that "the necessary legislative work to implement the regulation in Norwegian law is underway" -- a small but genuine advance on the July 21 announcement -- but no Prop. til Stortinget has been tabled and no horing specific to this incorporation has appeared. The stortinget.no case search still returns only historical 2023-24 horing records on the EU regulation's Council position and the unrelated March 2026 Prop. 80 L on exploitation of foreign workers. Note regjeringen.no intermittently blocks automated fetch (403); this run the content was reachable via search cache. So this remains a formal government decision with no domestic implementing instrument enacted, which is Partial under the standing policy. FALSE-CLAIM GUARD, now traced to source: a claim that Norway has requested WTO dispute consultations over the US tariff has surfaced on several runs and has never been corroborated; this run it was pinned down -- the regjeringen.no WTO consultation-request pages being cited (id2604315 and id2616344) are from the 2018 steel and aluminium dispute, not this action. NEW THIS RUN: Adresseavisen, August 19, 2026 reports a state secretary in the Norwegian Foreign Ministry saying after a meeting with US officials that the Americans are clear a prohibition in progress is insufficient -- it must be adopted and in force before tariff relief follows. That is a useful external confirmation of the distinction this tracker itself draws between a decision to legislate and an enacted instrument, and it underlines that Norway's Partial rests on a government decision with no Storting proposition yet tabled. Source: regjeringen.no, July 21, 2026; NRK and NTB/FriFagbevegelse, July 21-22, 2026; stortinget.no case search.

NEGATIVE UPGRADED TO DOCUMENT LEVEL ON SEPTEMBER 7: rather than inferring from news silence, a pass fetched the Storting's own "Saker som ventes fra regjeringen" list -- the register of propositions the government is expected to bring -- and it contains NO entry for a forced-labour or tvangsarbeid proposition and none for incorporating EU Regulation 2024/3015.
