Summary and Source: Peru's forced-labour import-ban bill was formally submitted to Congress on July 2, 2026 with "very urgent" status requested and referred to the Foreign Trade and Economy committees on July 6, but was never taken up: the Foreign Trade Commission closed its 2025-2026 session without addressing it and the Permanent Commission's term ended July 15. The new bicameral Congress (2026-2031) was seated July 28, 2026 and the bill remains unassigned. On the Executive's parallel route, Foreign Trade and Tourism Minister Rogers Valencia said a forced-labour import/dealings prohibition would be folded into the government's request to Congress for delegated legislative powers ("facultades legislativas"). PRECISION CORRECTION this run: this row previously stated that the Council of Ministers did not approve that request at its August 5 session. That overstated the sourcing. What the sources actually support is that the session was postponed from August 2 -- when the government said the "conditions do not exist" for approval and the proposal was still being refined at technical level -- and was rescheduled to August 5; no source reports the OUTCOME of the August 5 session. Re-checked in Spanish on August 15, 2026, including the official gazette elperuano.pe: the outcome of the August 5 session is STILL unreported by any source TEN DAYS later, and no Decreto Legislativo or Ley on forced-labour imports has been published -- renewed Spanish-language searching returns only the August 3 La Republica item confirming the session was scheduled, and an August 10 opinion column on delegated legislative powers generally, neither of which states whether the request was approved or reached Congress. FURTHER DETAIL THIS RUN, recorded with its tension flagged: Caretas reported on July 29, 2026 that the Executive was seeking delegated powers for 120 days across security, MYPEs, employment, formalisation, productive development, the tax regime, customs and trade facilitation -- but that report does NOT mention a forced-labour provision among the listed matters. Whether the forced-labour prohibition survived into the text actually put before Congress is therefore unconfirmed; it rests on Mincetur's separate statement of intent. Note also the apparent sequencing tension: that report predates the August 2 postponement and the August 5 session, so it is not treated here as evidence that the request has cleared the Council of Ministers. Re-checked August 19, 2026: the August 5 outcome remains unreported by any source FOURTEEN DAYS on. (A research pass this run put the gap at sixteen days; the arithmetic is wrong -- August 5 to August 19 is fourteen days -- and the row uses the correct figure.) NEW NEGATIVE CHECK, at the register rather than through news: congreso.gob.pe was searched directly and NO project number has been assigned to any delegated-powers or forced-labour bill, so there is still no evidence the request has been formally received by Congress. GAZETTE CHECKED AT THE DAY LEVEL this run: the El Peruano legal-norms digests for both August 5 and August 15, 2026 were examined and contain no Decreto Legislativo, Ley or delegated-powers instrument touching forced labour -- only routine ministerial and supreme resolutions. ONE CLAIM RECORDED BUT NOT ADOPTED: a search-engine synthesis of the August reporting asserts that the forced-labour import/dealings prohibition WAS included in the delegated-powers request discussed on August 5, which would resolve the open question of whether the clause survived into the submitted text. That synthesis is not a named, dated article and could not be traced to a primary source, and this row has been burned before by asserting more than the sources support, so the inclusion question stays OPEN rather than resolved. It rests, as before, only on Mincetur's separate statement of intent, and no Decreto Legislativo or Ley on forced-labour imports has been published. No approval, no confirmed submission carrying the forced-labour clause and no published measure through either route, so the classification is unchanged, and the row continues not to assert a negative decision that was never actually reported. Source: Congreso del Peru communications; Gestion, Infobae and Caretas, August 2-3, 2026; La Republica, August 3, 2026; RPP Noticias, July 24, 2026.
Official Forced Labor Import Ban: Partial (bill formally submitted to Congress July 2, 2026 and referred to the Foreign Trade and Economy committees July 6, never taken up, and still unassigned in the new bicameral Congress seated July 28, 2026. On the Executive route, the Council of Ministers approved the delegated-powers request on August 27, 2026 after five postponements -- verified directly from La Republica of that date -- and it was filed with the Camara de Diputados on August 28, 2026 as Oficio No. 245-2026-PR, seeking to legislate for 120 days across 66 specific requests. CORRECTION, REVERSING THIS ROW'S CONCLUSION OF AUGUST 29: yesterday this row recorded the forced-labour pathway as "CONFIRMED AND EFFECTIVELY CLOSED," on the basis that none of the 66 requests across eight areas concerned forced labour. THAT WAS WRONG, and the error was in reasoning from an absence in short press summaries to a positive finding of exclusion. The filed package DOES contain a forced-labour import prohibition. I verified this directly in two independent outlets on August 30. Infobae of August 29 lists among the tax-and-trade measures: "La prohibicion de importar mercancias elaboradas con trabajo forzoso, en linea con compromisos internacionales asumidos por el Peru." Gestion's detailed breakdown states: "La propuesta incorpora ademas medidas para impedir el ingreso al pais de mercancias elaboradas total o parcialmente mediante trabajo forzoso, incluyendo su prohibicion de importacion," placing it in the customs and trade-facilitation bloc rather than in a labour bloc -- which is why the earlier eight-area summaries, which named that bloc only as "temas tributarios," appeared to omit it. Mincetur Minister Rogers Valencia's pledge therefore DID survive into the delivered text, and this pathway is live, not closed. The classification is unchanged at Partial, because delegated powers are a request to legislate and not themselves a measure: no Decreto Legislativo has been issued and elperuano.pe carries no forced-labour instrument. But the basis is now materially stronger than at any previous point, and this is the likeliest route by which Peru reaches Yes. Two caveats kept: no project/expediente number for the August 28 filing could be located on congreso.gob.pe, so the filing rests on press reporting rather than the congressional record; and the forced-labour clause is confirmed from two independent secondary reports of the text, not from the filed text itself, which I have not been able to read. Re-checked August 31: the expediente number remains unfound -- congreso.gob.pe pages were not retrievable this run -- and no Decreto Legislativo has appeared. That last point is stated with its limit: busquedas.elperuano.pe was fetched and contains zero occurrences of "forzoso," but that is the search portal rather than the daily Normas Legales digests, so it is index-level evidence, not a document-level negative. THE REQUEST IS NOW PROCEDURALLY STUCK, AND I VERIFIED THIS DIRECTLY IN LA REPUBLICA OF AUGUST 30, 2026: despite being filed "con caracter de muy urgente," the Camara de Diputados "mantiene el proyecto en el limbo," and "el portal institucional no registra que la iniciativa haya sido derivada a la Comision de Constitucion, Reglamento y Relaciones Exteriores para darle el tramite correspondiente." The reason is a paperwork defect rather than a political vote: the Executive did not attach the acta substantiating the "muy urgente" classification. So the delegation is not merely awaiting a vote, it has not even been referred to committee. ONE CLAIM CHECKED AND NOT ADOPTED: a research pass reported the filing carries expediente "Project Law No. 00098-2026-2031-CD," which would finally answer a question open since August 28. I fetched BOTH sources it cited -- the La Republica piece above and the Infobae report of August 29 -- and the string "00098" appears in NEITHER. The number may well be right, but it is not supported by the sources given, so this row still records no verified expediente number. THE BLOCKER IS NOW CURED AND THE REQUEST HAS REACHED COMMITTEE -- verified directly in El Comercio on September 2. The Camara de Diputados president Oscar Reto had asked the Executive to supply the missing acta, noting that only "una vez subsanada la observacion, recien podra iniciarse el computo de los plazos previstos reglamentariamente." Minutes later it was reported that "el Poder Ejecutivo envio al Parlamento el Oficio N. 246-2026-PR, mediante el cual adjunto la copia certificada del acta de la sesion del Consejo de Ministros del 27 de agosto de 2026," in which the delegation request was approved UNANIMOUSLY and the Executive asked for urgent treatment. Reto then confirmed the request "sera derivado, en la fecha, a la Comision de Constitucion y Reglamento." That Commission, chaired by Giannina Avendano (Juntos por el Peru), has declared itself EN SESION PERMANENTE to deal with it. So in three days this went from "en el limbo" to referred and in permanent session -- the fastest movement this row has seen. TWO CORRECTIONS TO THIS ROW'S OWN RECORD. First, the Oficio number: this row has stated the August 28 filing was "Oficio No. 245-2026-PR," which came from a research pass and which I never verified; the number I have now verified in a primary news text is 246-2026-PR, and it belongs to the SUPPLEMENTARY transmittal carrying the acta, not necessarily to the original filing. A research pass suggested 246 "supersedes" 245; that is an over-reading -- a follow-up oficio attaching a missing annex does not replace the original. So: 246 is verified as the acta transmittal, 245 remains unverified as the filing number, and neither should be asserted beyond that. Second, there is still NO expediente/project number, and the "00098-2026-2031-CD" figure rejected on September 1 has not reappeared in any source. SEPTEMBER 3 UPDATE: the Comision de Constitucion voted 18-2 to declare itself in permanent session and plans to summon Executive ministers for hearings. That is a scheduling posture, not a decision on content -- no debate, amendment or vote on the substance has yet occurred. THE LIVE RISK TO THIS ROW IS NOW NAMED PRECISELY: commissions routinely trim delegated-powers requests, so the question is whether the forced-labour import prohibition survives the commission stage. Nothing found suggests it has been excised -- the reporting on the package still lists it -- but nothing confirms it will survive either, and that is the specific thing to watch rather than the delegation as a whole. Classification stays Partial: a referral to committee is procedural progress, not a measure. September 4 check: no committee debate, ministerial hearing, amendment or vote has been reported since the permanent-session declaration, and no plenary vote has occurred -- so the trimming question remains genuinely open rather than resolved either way. El Peruano was checked at DIGEST level rather than via the search portal this time: the Normas Legales listing for September 3 returned "No se encontro informacion," so no Decreto Legislativo or Ley on forced labour has been published. Still no expediente number, and the rejected "00098-2026-2031-CD" has not resurfaced. September 5: no dictamen, ministerial hearing, debate, amendment or committee vote has occurred, and no plenary vote -- the trimming question is still open. The El Peruano Normas Legales digest for September 4 was read at day level (76 norms: budget bills, supreme decrees, ministerial and directoral resolutions, JNE resolutions, appointments) and contains no Decreto Legislativo, Ley or forced-labour measure; the September 5 digest was not yet retrievable, which is a gap rather than a negative. STALE-SOURCE TRAP CAUGHT AGAIN: two search results headlined around the Comision de Constitucion and "Pleno delega facultades" looked like a live dictamen and turned out to date from 2024 and 2021 respectively. This row has now been offered stale Peruvian delegation articles three separate times. SEPTEMBER 6 ADDS A CLOCK, which this row has lacked. Committee chair Giannina Avendano is reported as clarifying that once the request is properly regularised, deputies have "hasta 15 dias habiles" to issue their dictamen. That converts an open-ended wait into a bounded one and gives the trimming question a horizon: a dictamen is now expected within roughly three working weeks of regularisation, and it is the dictamen that will show whether the forced-labour import prohibition survived. Still no dictamen, no ministerial hearing, no debate, no committee vote and no plenary vote. The El Peruano Normas Legales digest was read at day level for September 5 and returned "No se encontro informacion"; the September 6 digest was not separately retrievable, which is a gap rather than a negative. What moves this row to Yes is a Decreto Legislativo issued under the delegation and published in El Peruano)

Summary and Source: On July 24, 2026, the Philippines' Trade, Labor, and Finance departments signed a Joint Administrative Order (JAO) establishing an inter-agency committee (DTI chair, DOLE vice-chair, plus DOF, Bureau of Customs, BOI, PEZA) to receive, investigate, and act on forced-labor-import complaints under existing customs-law authority (RA 10863); Trade Secretary Cristina Roque called it a measure to protect "people and...fair competition." This is an enacted administrative order but functions as an investigation/enforcement mechanism referencing existing law rather than a standalone blanket import prohibition, so it is classified Partial rather than Yes. USTR's July 23, 2026 final Section 301 determination confirmed a final tariff of 12.5% for the Philippines (the JAO was signed the day after the determination, so it was not credited in the tier assignment). NEW this run: Philippine officials are lobbying Washington to cut the 12.5% tariff to 10%, citing the JAO as the qualifying measure; no change to the classification, which turns on the instrument, not on the tier sought. Source: Manila Times, BusinessWorld, July 23-24, 2026; USTR press release, July 23, 2026.
Official Forced Labor Import Ban: Partial (Joint Administrative Order signed July 24, 2026, establishing an inter-agency forced-labor-import investigation/enforcement mechanism under existing customs law; not itself a standalone blanket import prohibition. NEW: House Bill No. 10848, "An Act Prohibiting the Trade of Goods Produced Wholly or in Part with Forced Labor and Providing Penalties Therefor," filed by Albay Rep. Joey Salceda, would create a standalone statutory import prohibition with Bureau of Customs exclusion and forfeiture powers and would put the JAO mechanism on a statutory footing. It is filed and numbered but NOT enacted, so it independently supports Partial rather than changing it -- and it is the first Philippine legislative vehicle that could later carry this row to Yes)

Source: Public Television Service (PTS) and Executive Yuan Section 301 portal, July 29-30, 2026; Amnesty International Taiwan; Ministry of Labor (Taiwan, official), July 30, 2026; Newtalk and Taipei Times, July 30-31, 2026; USTR fact sheet, February 2026.

RECLASSIFICATION TO PARTIAL PROPOSED THIS RUN, CONSIDERED SERIOUSLY, AND REJECTED ON THE PRIMARY TEXT. A research pass argued the June 2026 Cabinet decision satisfies the standing policy's Partial limb (iv), "a formal government decision with instrument pending." That is a fair question, so I read the Thai government's own account -- the Public Relations Department release -- rather than the secondary summaries. It says the Cabinet "มีมติเห็นชอบตามที่กระทรวงแรงงานเสนอ ในการกำหนดหลักเกณฑ์สินค้านำเข้าที่มีความเสี่ยงการใช้แรงงานบังคับ" and approved TWO things: acknowledging the investigation findings, and approving the ESTABLISHMENT of a "คณะกรรมการกำหนดมาตรฐานสินค้านำเข้าที่มีความเสี่ยงจากการบังคับใช้แรงงานหรือบริการ" chaired by the Labour Minister. So the decision creates a BODY THAT WILL LATER PROPOSE measures; it is not itself a decision to adopt a measure with an instrument merely awaiting publication. No list has been proposed, let alone approved or gazetted, and the phrase "ห้ามนำเข้า" (prohibit import) appears ZERO times in either account. That places Thailand alongside South Africa's announced intent to consult rather than alongside a pending instrument, so it stays No. This is a considered judgment on a genuinely arguable point, not a brush-off: if the committee proposes a Risk List and the Cabinet approves it, or a Section 5 Royal Gazette notice issues, this row moves)

Summary and Source: The specific domestic instrument has now been located and verified directly: Trinidad and Tobago's Finance Act, 2026 (Act No. 16 of 2026), assented to on 25 June 2026 and published in Legal Supplement Part A to the Trinidad and Tobago Gazette, Vol. 65, No. 111, 29 June 2026, section 24 amends the Customs Act (Chap. 78:01) section 45(1) by inserting a new paragraph: "(w) all goods produced from forced labour as designated by the Minister with responsibility for trade". Section 45(1) is the Customs Act's list of prohibited/restricted imports, so this is a genuine, enacted, gazetted forced-labor import prohibition (designation-dependent -- the specific list of goods is left to the Minister with responsibility for trade to designate, similar in structure to several other economies' framework-style bans). This confirms and supersedes the prior entry's reliance on USTR's Federal Register final-action notice (which had stated, without naming the instrument, that Trinidad and Tobago "adopt[ed] a forced labor import prohibition subsequent to the publication of the June 5, 2026 FRN" -- the Finance Act's 25 June 2026 assent date fits neatly within that window). USTR's final action (July 23, 2026) placed Trinidad and Tobago in the 10% tariff tier on this basis. Source: Trinidad and Tobago e-Gazette (printery.gov.tt), Finance Act 2026 (Act No. 16 of 2026), 29 June 2026; USTR Federal Register final-action notice, July 23, 2026.

Summary and Source: USTR credited the UK with a "partial regime" (2023 Procurement Act forced-labour exclusions, 2025 Great British Energy Act provisions), securing the 10% tier. No government import-ban bill has been tabled: bills.parliament.uk shows only the Import of Products of Forced Labour from Xinjiang (Prohibition) Bill, a narrow private member's bill; the Joint Committee on Human Rights report and the Independent Anti-Slavery Commissioner's December 2025 "model legislative drafting" report are advisory; and the Employment Rights Act 2025 (Fair Work Agency) is domestic enforcement, not an import measure. STALE/FALSE-POSITIVE GUARD: NEW THIS RUN, AND IT REFINES THE OLD GUARD RATHER THAN OVERTURNING IT: the government DID introduce a bill on June 30, 2026 -- the Immigration and Asylum Bill (bills.parliament.uk/bills/4254), which passed second reading on July 13, 2026 by 264 to 90 and carries real amendments to Modern Slavery Act section 54 transparency-in-supply-chains duties: broadened scope, mandatory content criteria and financial penalties reported at up to GBP 1m or 1% of turnover. So a June 30 government bill exists after all. It is NOT, however, an import-ban bill: TISC provisions are corporate disclosure and reporting obligations, so the classification is unchanged, and the original guard still holds for what it actually addressed -- namely that no forced-labour IMPORT-PROHIBITION bill was introduced that day. Both halves are recorded because the near-miss between them is exactly what caused the earlier confusion. For completeness the old guard: search results have surfaced a claim that the government "introduced a bill on June 30, 2026" -- that traces to the Business and Trade Committee hearing at which Bryant made those remarks, NOT to any bill introduction, and no such bill appears on the parliamentary register. Do not treat it as a tabled government measure. SOURCING LIMIT STATED PLAINLY, TWO DAYS BEFORE THE SEPTEMBER 4 LORDS DEBATE: the amendment paper could not be reached for a THIRD consecutive run. I tried bills.parliament.uk/bills/4254/publications, publications.parliament.uk and lordslibrary.parliament.uk myself on September 2 and all three returned HTTP 403, and a research pass additionally got 403 from the JCHR committee page. No secondary source, and no search result, describes any import-prohibition amendment -- every account still frames the bill's forced-labour content as strengthened Modern Slavery Act s.54 TISC disclosure duties (broadened scope, mandatory content, penalties up to GBP 1m or 1% of turnover). So the honest position is that no such amendment is REPORTED, but it cannot be ruled in or out against the primary text, because the primary text is unreachable. THAT POSITION IMPROVED MATERIALLY ON SEPTEMBER 3, THE DAY BEFORE THE LORDS DEBATE, and the improvement is in the KIND of evidence rather than the volume. Until now the negative rested on silence -- no source mentioning an import-prohibition amendment. Anti-Slavery International's own campaign page on this Bill now supplies POSITIVE evidence of absence: it criticises the Bill precisely for "the absence of a forced labour import ban," notes that the Independent Anti-Slavery Commissioner's December 2025 model legislation DID include an import ban and has not been adopted, and describes the Bill's Part 5 forced-labour provisions as confined to Modern Slavery Act s.54 disclosure duties. An advocacy organisation campaigning FOR an import ban, complaining that this Bill lacks one, is much stronger evidence than silence. The parliamentary sources remain blocked -- bills.parliament.uk, publications.parliament.uk, lordslibrary.parliament.uk and the JCHR page all returned HTTP 403 for a FOURTH consecutive run, several of which I retried myself -- so the amendment paper itself is still unread, and a late-tabled Lords amendment could not be seen this way. But the classification rests on firmer ground than it did. THE SEPTEMBER 4 LORDS SITTING HAPPENED, AND IT WAS NOT WHAT THIS ROW EXPECTED -- a useful correction of framing rather than of classification. The Lords debated the Joint Committee on Human Rights REPORT "Forced Labour in UK Supply Chains" (published July 2025), not a Committee-stage amendment sitting on the Bill; the Public Bill Committee first sits on September 10. JCHR Chair Lord Alton welcomed the Bill's strengthened TISC provisions -- broadened s.54 scope reaching some public authorities, mandated statement content, and penalties up to GBP 1m or 1% of turnover. NO import-prohibition amendment was tabled, moved or spoken to, on any account found. Two honest limits: this rests on secondary summaries because the Hansard transcript for the sitting could not be reached -- I tried hansard.parliament.uk myself and got HTTP 403, and theyworkforyou.com returned 418 -- and the amendment paper remains blocked for a FIFTH consecutive run. So a late-tabled amendment still could not be excluded from the primary record, though nothing in any accessible source suggests one. Only an import prohibition would change this row. Source: UK Parliament (bills.parliament.uk) and House of Lords Library; Independent Anti-Slavery Commissioner, December 2025; Export Compliance Daily, July 1, 2026.

Summary and Source: Vietnam's Government issued Decree No. 292/2026/ND-CP on July 22, 2026, implementing the Law on Foreign Trade Management; item 23 of its Appendix I prohibited-import list bans "products and goods extracted, produced, or manufactured wholly or partly through forced labor." Effective September 5, 2026 (45 days after issuance). Vietnam's Foreign Ministry separately rejected USTR's findings and reiterated that Vietnam "strictly prohibits all forms of forced labour." IMPLEMENTATION MECHANISM PINNED DOWN this run: per Article 5(2) of the decree, ministries and ministerial-level agencies are tasked with announcing the detailed HS-code-level goods lists built on Appendix I -- so the decree is self-executing as a prohibition but depends on those ministerial lists for operational scope. Re-checked in Vietnamese on September 7, 2026 -- the third day the decree has been in force: no ministerial HS-code list, no implementing circular (thong tu) and no General Department of Customs preparation notice has been published. WATCH ITEM NOW RESOLVED: yesterday's single-source claim that the forced-labour category is administered by the Ministry of Interior/Home Affairs (Bo Noi vu) rather than a trade ministry has been corroborated by multiple independent Vietnamese sources (luatvietnam.vn, congluan.vn, vietnam.vn) citing Appendix I of the decree directly ("nhom hang hoa nay do Bo Noi vu quan ly"). It is therefore adopted rather than merely flagged. This matters practically: it identifies which body must issue the Article 5(2) HS-code list, and it is an unusual assignment for an import-control category, so the list is not to be expected from the trade ministry. Note the decree predated USTR's July 23 final determination by one day yet Vietnam was still placed in the 12.5% tier. Source: Bao Chinh Phu (Vietnam Government Portal), July 22-23, 2026; Lao Dong; LuatVietnam and RBV, July-August 2026.
Official Forced Labor Import Ban: Yes (Decree No. 292/2026/ND-CP, issued July 22, 2026, Appendix I item 23; effective September 5, 2026, with the ministerial HS-code goods lists required by Article 5(2), any implementing circular, and customs preparation notices all still unpublished as of August 31, five days before the effective date; the goods category is administered by the Ministry of Interior (Bo Noi vu) per Appendix I, corroborated across multiple Vietnamese sources. AS OF SEPTEMBER 1 -- FOUR DAYS OUT -- THE GAP IS STILL OPEN, and Vietnamese reporting now acknowledges it rather than glossing over it: an August 31 analysis tells businesses they must "ra soat danh muc hang hoa dang kinh doanh, cap nhat ma HS do cac bo, nganh cong bo" -- review their goods and update HS codes ONCE THE MINISTRIES ANNOUNCE THEM -- which is direct confirmation from the Vietnamese side that those lists do not yet exist. baochinhphu.vn's own round-up of policies taking effect in September 2026 mentions the decree and no implementing instrument. I also fetched customs.gov.vn directly on August 31: its homepage carries zero mentions of the decree or "cuong buc," which is a homepage-level negative rather than a document-level one. The classification stays Yes, since the tracker's policy counts an enacted instrument even before it is operational, but a decree taking effect with no HS-code list, no circular and no customs notice is the single largest unresolved question in this tracker. So the decree will take effect on September 5 running on Appendix I's general language alone, with HS-code specificity and customs operational guidance both absent. That is the state of play at the wire. RE-CONFIRMED ON SEPTEMBER 4, THE DAY BEFORE IT BITES: no eleventh-hour circular, ministerial HS list or customs notice has appeared. Vietnamese coverage does not explain how enforcement is meant to function from September 5 without the Article 5(2) list. A DOWNGRADE TO PARTIAL WAS PROPOSED THIS RUN AND IS REJECTED: the standing policy is explicit that Yes covers an actually enacted instrument EVEN IF NOT YET FULLY EFFECTIVE, and an operational gap in implementation is not the same thing as the instrument not existing -- the decree is issued, published and in force from tomorrow. Vietnam stays Yes. The pass that proposed the downgrade in fact conceded the decree 'satisfies Yes-type criteria as issued', which is the whole point. THE DECREE IS NOW IN FORCE. September 5, 2026 arrived and Decree 292/2026/ND-CP took effect on schedule, replacing Decree 69/2018/ND-CP -- and NO implementing instrument appeared at the moment of effect. No thong tu, no Bo Noi vu HS-code list, no Tong cuc Hai quan notice, no importer guidance, no shipment holds and no law-firm client alert dated the effective date could be found. I re-fetched customs.gov.vn myself today: zero occurrences of 'cuong buc', '292' or 'cam nhap khau' on the homepage. I also read luatvietnam.vn's own text of the prohibited-goods list directly, which confirms item 23 verbatim -- 'Cac san pham, hang hoa duoc khai thac, san xuat hoac che tao toan bo hoac mot phan boi hanh vi cuong buc lao dong tu cac doanh nghiep, quoc gia, vung lanh tho...' with Bo Noi vu named as the responsible ministry -- and the string 'ma HS' appears ZERO times anywhere in that article. WHY THE GAP MATTERS MORE THAN IT DID YESTERDAY: Vietnamese reporting states the operative rule as 'viec xac dinh hang cam nhap khau phai can cu ma so HS va mo ta chi tiet hang hoa trong danh muc do bo truong, thu truong co quan ngang bo co tham quyen cong bo' -- identifying a prohibited good MUST be based on the HS code and detailed description in the ministerial list. If that is right, then until Bo Noi vu publishes, customs has a prohibition in force with no operative means of identifying what falls under it. Vietnam remains Yes -- the instrument is enacted, published and now in force, which is exactly what the standing policy asks -- but the tracker should stop describing this as a pending implementation question and start describing it as a live enforceability question.
